name: The Moreton Bay Fig of Balboa Park

location.address: North entrance plaza, San Diego Natural History Museum, Balboa Park, San Diego, CA

access: Free, in the open park outside the Natural History Museum. The ground beneath its crown has been fenced off since 1989 to protect the tree's surface roots from foot traffic, but the tree itself is fully visible from the plaza.
transport: Served by MTS bus route 7 to Balboa Park (Park Blvd pedestrian overpass stop), about a 10 minute walk to the museum plaza.
verify_notes: Planted 1914 as a five-gallon sapling for the 1915 Panama-California Exposition's San Diego County garden exhibit; as of 2017 the Nat's own history calls it the last surviving plant from that exhibit. Age counted from planting (1914) rather than exposition opening. 1996 measurements from the California Registry of Big Trees, cited by the Nat: height ~78 ft (24 m), crown width ~123 ft (37 m), trunk girth 486 in (12.3 m) -- note girth is a buttressed fig mass, not a single round trunk, so do not repeat it as a simple diameter figure. Declined from soil compaction and root damage from visitors; trimmed and fenced off in 1989, has since recovered and now shows characteristic aerial roots. The Nat's own page explicitly flags an unverified attribution: 'While some attribute the planting to Kate Sessions... there is no documentation to verify this claim' -- do NOT credit Sessions with this specific tree, that would be the bridge-claim trap. One of California's largest trees per the Big Tree registry. Flagged only because the 1996 measurement is three decades old; the tree's survival and continued presence are otherwise well documented (Wikipedia, the Nat's own current page, San Diego Reader 2017 piece).

name: The Kate Sessions Tipu Tree
species: Pride of Bolivia / Tipu Tree (Tipuana tipu)
age_estimate: about a century old, planted in the 1920s

location.address: Northwest corner of Garnet Avenue and Pico Street, Pacific Beach, San Diego, CA (California Historical Landmark No. 764)

access: Free, on a public street corner. The tree and its California Historical Landmark plaque stand in the open on the northwest corner of Garnet Avenue and Pico Street.
transport: Served by MTS bus routes through Pacific Beach on Garnet Avenue; roughly a 10 minute walk from the Mission Bay Dr / Garnet Ave corridor.
verify_notes: Kate Sessions, San Diego's pioneering horticulturist ('Mother of Balboa Park'), bought 7 acres at Garnet and Pico in Pacific Beach in the 1920s (one source gives 1924 for the purchase) for her final nursery, Soledad Terrace. The tipu tree she planted there is the only survivor of that nursery; it now grows beside California Historical Landmark No. 764, dedicated in 1961 to the nursery site itself (the plaque commemorates her life, not the tree specifically). katestrees.org (a site maintained by a Sessions researcher) dates the tree's planting to 1928 and calls it a protected heritage tree, still alive; the California Historical Landmarks blog gives 'planted in the 1920s', consistent with 1928. Landmark coordinates (32 48.325 N, 117 13.377 W) mark the plaque at the corner; sources describe the tree as standing near the marker rather than giving the tree's own coordinates, hence approximate precision. No girth or height found in any source checked. This is a directly documented Sessions planting (not a bridge claim): multiple sources independently name her as the planter of this specific tree, unlike the Balboa Park fig where the Sessions attribution is explicitly unverified.

name: The Guadalupe Island Cypress by the Horseshoe Club
species: Guadalupe Island Cypress (Hesperocyparis guadalupensis / Cupressus guadalupensis)

location.address: By the San Diego Chess Club and Horseshoe Club building, 2225 6th Avenue, Balboa Park, San Diego, CA (Sixth Avenue near Ivy Street)

access: Free, in the open park along Balboa Park's Sixth Avenue frontage, beside the public chess and horseshoe club building.
transport: On the Sixth Avenue side of Balboa Park; served by MTS bus route 3, about a 5 to 10 minute walk from the Cabrillo Bridge / Balboa Park west entrance area.
verify_notes: One of Kate Sessions' own plantings from her 1892 lease of park land at Sixth and Upas, in exchange for planting 100 trees a year (the same lease documented for sdg_002 and the cork oaks below). The Nat's own Sessions biography and San Diego Magazine (2020, 'What's the Oldest Tree in San Diego?') both independently name this species and location, describing it as 'enormously tall' and among the oldest confirmed Sessions plantings still standing, San Diego Magazine giving 'approximately 128 years old' as of 2020 (so roughly 134 by 2026; used a slightly broader band here to stay honest about the rough age). Guadalupe Island cypress is critically rare in the wild on its native Isla Guadalupe (threatened historically by feral goats), which makes a mainland specimen this size and age unusual. No girth or height measurement found in either source. Coordinates are my own estimate of the Sixth Avenue/Ivy Street area by the chess and horseshoe clubs (address 2225 6th Ave, confirmed by the chess club's own site) rather than a sourced tree-level position, hence approximate precision; a future pass should confirm the exact spot on the ground or via a mapped photo. sandiegoreader.com's 2017 'top ten trees of Balboa Park' piece likely covers this tree too but the host returned HTTP 403 (Cloudflare) on every fetch attempt (direct WebFetch, curl with browser UA, Wayback Machine copy, and a reader-proxy), so it could not be used; worth flagging for the blocklist.

name: The Kauri by the Mingei Museum

location.address: Beside the Mingei International Museum (House of Charm), Plaza de Panama, Balboa Park, San Diego, CA

verified_sources: https://www.sandiegoreader.com/news/2017/nov/22/cover-top-ten-trees-balboa-park/ (existence/species corroborated only via search result summary, page itself returned HTTP 403; treat with the caution below)
access: Free, in the open plaza outside the Mingei International Museum. No admission needed to see the tree itself; the museum charges for entry to its galleries.
transport: Central Balboa Park, on the Plaza de Panama; served by MTS bus route 7 to the Prado, about a 10 minute walk.
verify_notes: Kauri (Agathis australis) is a New Zealand species almost never seen in Southern California cultivation, which is what makes a specimen here notable regardless of its exact size. Existence, species and approximate position confirmed directly via a geotagged, photographed iNaturalist observation (id 342689280, 2016-07-09, 'Balboa Park, San Diego, CA', coordinates 32.7313561, -117.1511082, single observation, no other Agathis australis records found near San Diego on iNaturalist), which sits right beside the Mingei/House of Charm building as the press reports describe. CAUTION on everything else: multiple outlets (San Diego Reader's 2017 'top ten trees of Balboa Park', a Pacific Horticulture piece on New Zealand plants) independently discuss what is almost certainly this same tree and call it possibly 'the most valuable plant in the park', but both hosts returned HTTP 403 on every fetch attempt (direct fetch, browser-UA curl, Wayback Machine, and a reader proxy), so their specific numbers (a height around 65 ft per one source, 52 ft measured in 1994 per another, a planting estimate of 'late 1930s or early 1940s') come only from search-result summaries, not from the page itself, and per this project's own rule on search-summary figures they are NOT recorded as facts here. A future session that can browse past Cloudflare should re-verify age, height and the 'Agnes' nickname mentioned in search results before a writer uses any of them. Age and height left empty rather than guessed. Both blocked hosts are worth adding to the fetch blocklist: sandiegoreader.com and pacifichorticulture.org.
